nodes.title: Hitachi Energy CoreTec Product
nodes.tldr: View CSAF Summary Hitachi Energy is aware of OS command injection and Dirty Frag vulnerabilities that affect CoreTec product versions listed in this document. Successful exploitati...
nodes.details: View CSAF Summary Hitachi Energy is aware of OS command injection and Dirty Frag vulnerabilities that affect CoreTec product versions listed in this document. Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could result in impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability of the product. Please refer to the Recommended Immediate Actions for information about the mitigation/remediation. The following versions of Hitachi Energy CoreTec Product are affected: CoreTec5 vers:CoreTec5/<=3.4.0, 5.0.0 (CVE-2026-13162, CVE-2026-43284) CoreTec4 vers:CoreTec4/<=3.4.0 (CVE-2026-13162) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 8.8 Hitachi Energy CoreTec5 2 Vulnerabilities Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection'), Write-what-where Condition Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Energy Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Switzerland Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-13162 An OS command vulnerability exists in CoreTec product that allows authenticated users with certain roles to execute arbitrary system commands with full control over the device. The vulnerability exists in the configuration daemon's time synchronization handler, which is responsible for setting the system timezone. When processing timezone configuration updates, the daemon constructs a shell command by concatenating user-supplied input without any sanitization or validation. Read More 2 Affected Products CoreTec5 versions 3.4.0 and prior Product Status: fixed, known_affected, recommended Remediations Vendor fixUpdate to CoreTec5 version 5.0.0 CoreTec4 versions 3.4.0 and prior Product Status: fixed, known_affected, recommended Remediations Vendor fixUpgrade to CoreTec5 version 5.0.0 MitigationFollow general mitigation factors Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-78 Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection') CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 7.5 HIGH CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H 4.0 7.7 HIGH CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:H/AT:N/PR:L/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N View CVE Details CVE-2026-43284 A vulnerability exists in the IPsec ESP subsystem (esp4) of the Linux kernel used in CoreTec5 that allows a local unprivileged user to escalate privileges to root. The flaw exists in how the kernel handles memory pages when processing ESP encrypted network packets. An attacker can craft a packet that causes the kernel to decrypt data directly into memory pages it does not own, including cached copies of privileged operating system binaries. When one of those binaries is executed, the attacker's injected code runs with root privileges. In CoreTec5, the vulnerable ESP component is compiled in kernel as a built-in and is present at boot time allowing a local user to exploit it. Read More 3 Affected Products CoreTec5 versions 3.4.0 and prior Product Status: fixed, known_affected, recommended Remediations Vendor fixUpdate to CoreTec5 version 5.0.0 CoreTec4 versions 3.4.0 and prior Product Status: fixed, known_affected, recommended Remediations CoreTec5 versions 3.4.0 and prior Product Status: fixed, known_affected, recommended Remediations Vendor fixUpdate to CoreTec5 version 5.0.0 Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-123 Write-what-where Condition CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 8.8 HIGH CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H View CVE Details Acknowledgments Ritesh Kumar Kalle, Subhojeet Mukherjee, Hishamudeen of the Cybersecurity Research group, Hitachi India R&D Center reported these vulnerabilities to CISA. In no event shall Hitachi Energy or any of its suppliers be liable for direct, indirect, special, incidental or consequential damages of any nature or kind arising from the use of this document, or from the use of any hardware or software described in this document, even if Hitachi Energy or its suppliers have been advised of the possibility of such damages. This document and parts hereof must not be reproduced or copied without written permission from Hitachi Energy and the contents hereof must not be imparted to a third party nor used for any unauthorized purpose. All rights to registrations and trademarks reside with their respective owners. Support For additional information and support please contact your product provider or Hitachi Energy service organization. For contact information, see https://www.hitachienergy.com/contact-us/ for Hitachi Energy contact-centers. General Mitigation Factors Recommended security practices and firewall configurations can help protect a process control network from attacks that originate from outside the network. Such practices include that process control systems are physically protected from direct access by unauthorized personnel, have no direct connections to the Internet, and are separated from other networks by means of a firewall system that has a minimal number of ports exposed, and others that have to be evaluated case by case. Process control systems should not be used for Internet surfing, instant messaging, or receiving e-mails. Portable computers and removable storage media should be carefully scanned for viruses before they are connected to a control system. Proper password policies and processes should be followed. Additional information on Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity Best Practices can be found in the Hitachi Energy “Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity Best Practices” Cybersecurity Notification. [1] SSVC SSVCv2/E:N/A:N/2026-10-26T15:17:24Z/ Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. nodes.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
nodes.tldr: CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-97229 GitLab Community Edition and E...
nodes.details: CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-97229 GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition Integer Overflow or Wraparound vulnerability CVE-2026-76418 Cisco Secure Firewall ASA Software and Cisco Secure FTD Software Unchecked Return Value to NULL Pointer Dereference Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.  Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.  While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.  Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. nodes.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
nodes.tldr: CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-41709 Broadcom VMWare ESX Insufficie...
nodes.details: CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-41709 Broadcom VMWare ESX Insufficient Logging Vulnerability CVE-2026-46300 Linux Kernel Missing Initialization of a Variable Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.  Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.  While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.  Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

nodes.title: Commission accepts Temu's action plan to remedy the breach of the Digital Services Act
nodes.tldr: Commission accepts Temu's action plan to remedy the breach of the Digital Services Act Anonymous (not verified) Mon, 10/26/2026 - 10:28 The European Commission has accepted Temu's ...
nodes.details: Commission accepts Temu's action plan to remedy the breach of the Digital Services Act Anonymous (not verified) Mon, 10/26/2026 - 10:28 The European Commission has accepted Temu's action plan to comply with the Digital Services Act (DSA) and tackle the availability of illegal products online. Temu's plan focuses on five measures to remedy its breach of the DSA. The company will carry out a platform-specific risk analysis. It will also use reliable metrics to evaluate the effectiveness of the mitigation measures put in place in reducing the risk of dissemination of illegal content. The platform will assess the limitations of its content moderation and analyse whether, and how, its recommender systems may amplify the spread of illegal goods. Additionally, Temu will examine the influence of intentional manipulation and amplification of illegal items, including by sellers exploiting Temu's features to spread potentially illegal listings. The company now has four months to conduct an interim risk assessment that covers a six-month period, until 30 November 2026, to ensure the implementation of the measures of the action plan. The action plan is another example of how the DSA is enhancing consumer protection online and limiting the spread of illegal products in Europe. The action plan was submitted following a non-compliance decision in May 2026, in which the Commission found that Temu had failed to comply with its risk assessment obligations, and issued a €200 million fine. Read more about Temu's corrective measures to terminate breach of the DSA. nodes.title: Digital Services Act study on financial scams on online platforms and ways to counter them
nodes.tldr: Digital Services Act study on financial scams on online platforms and ways to counter them Anonymous (not verified) Tue, 10/20/2026 - 08:47 A new study maps the main types of onlin...
nodes.details: Digital Services Act study on financial scams on online platforms and ways to counter them Anonymous (not verified) Tue, 10/20/2026 - 08:47 A new study maps the main types of online financial scams, platform features scammers exploit, their impact on users and society and measures platforms can take to stop them. Online financial scams – fraudulent schemes whose primary aim is to extract money from victims – have grown into a pervasive crime in the digital age. They are present across all types of online intermediary services, including Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) and Very Large Search Engines (VLOSEs). The European Commission has procured this study in 2025 to support its supervisory and enforcement tasks under the Digital Services Act (DSA). It provides a typological mapping of financial scam formats across online platforms and assesses existing and emerging mitigation strategies to curb financial scams online. The study was carried out by Open Evidence and Spark Legal and Policy Consulting. It does not evaluate compliance by providers of VLOPs and VLOSEs. Read the study and the executive summary in (French and English). Key insights A diverse typology of scams The study maps different types of online financial scams and categorises them in six broad categories: investment scams romance scams e-commerce scams employment and collaboration scams unexpected gain scams disaster relief scams The study finds that investment scams and romance scams are the most common and fastest-growing forms of scams in Europe. It also finds that the scam landscape is increasingly being redefined by overlapping methods across different categories. Online platforms features and financial scams The study presents information on relevant features related to scams on online platforms including: advertising systems recommender systems content moderation of organic content monetisation systems app store content and private messaging functions inauthentic identities and account manipulation deceptive commercial content generative AI The study also shows how financial scams operate across different platforms and are facilitated by organised criminal networks that sell tools and services, effectively lowering the barrier to entry. Identifying effective countermeasures The study identifies relevant countermeasures across 4 categories: Access and gatekeeping measures, such as know your business customer and identity requirements are the first line of defence against online financial scams; Detection and removal measures, including automated and human-review based measures, can neutralise scam content; User facing measures – such as reporting tools and information on redress – can equip end users with tools and information to identify and report online scams; Platform-level policies and cooperation with third parties can help platforms identify, prevent and address online scams. Find further information about Fighting online scams with the DSA. Related topics Online platforms and e-commerce DSA - Digital Services Act

nodes.title: First harmonised standard supporting the AI Act published in the Official Journal
nodes.tldr: First harmonised standard supporting the AI Act published in the Official Journal Anonymous (not verified) Mon, 10/19/2026 - 09:37 The European Commission has published the referen...
nodes.details: First harmonised standard supporting the AI Act published in the Official Journal Anonymous (not verified) Mon, 10/19/2026 - 09:37 The European Commission has published the reference to the first harmonised standard supporting the implementation of the AI Act in the Official Journal of the European Union. The standard, EN 18286:2026 - Artificial intelligence - Quality management system for EU AI Act regulatory purposes, developed by CEN and CENELEC, provides a clear legal pathway for providers of high-risk AI systems to comply with the quality management system requirements under article 17 of the AI Act. Its publication through Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2274 means that providers implementing this standard will benefit from a presumption of conformity with the Article 17 requirements covered by the standard. EN 18286 translates these requirements into an operational quality management system (QMS). It is the only AI QMS standard with a presumption of conformity. It is mapped to Article 17 of the AI Act, built around the AI system lifecycle – rather than the organisation – and designed to be layered on top of the existing international standards – such as ISO/IEC 42001, ISO 9001 or a sectoral QMS (e.g. ISO 13485) – rather than replace them.  EN 18286 explicitly allows providers in regulated sectors to integrate management systems, rather than run separate ones. Organisations without ISO/IEC 42001 that plan to place or put into service high-risk AI systems in the EU market can use EN 18286 to expand an existing QMS or build one that fulfills the requirements of article 17 requirements. The publication of this standard marks an important milestone in implementing the AI Act, ahead of the application of requirements for high-risk AI systems, with further harmonised standards expected to follow. Find further information about the Standardisation of the AI Act. Related topics Artificial intelligence
